nameStory: These magnificent whales earned their 'pilot' name from early whalers who noticed how one whale seemed to 'pilot' or lead the entire group, with others following closely behind. The 'long-finned' part comes from their unusually long pectoral fins, which can stretch up to one-fifth of their total body length. Sailors sometimes called them 'pothead whales' due to their distinctive rounded, bulbous heads.
description: Long-finned pilot whales are actually large oceanic dolphins, despite their name! These impressive marine mammals can reach 12-20 feet in length and are jet black or dark gray all over. They have a distinctive bulging forehead called a melon and an almost non-existent beak, giving them a unique rounded profile. Their most striking feature is their exceptionally long, curved pectoral fins that sweep back along their sleek bodies.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Large, robust body 12-20 feet long with a distinctively bulging, rounded forehead and almost no visible beak - the head looks like a smooth, inflated balloon

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Exceptionally long, curved pectoral fins that can be up to 4 feet long - much longer than other whales of similar size, sweeping back like elegant black wings

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Uniformly jet black or very dark gray all over, sometimes with a lighter gray anchor-shaped patch on the chest that's hard to see from a distance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Travel in tight family groups of 10-30 individuals, often swimming in coordinated formations and frequently spy-hopping (poking heads straight up out of water)

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deep, cold offshore waters, rarely coming close to shore except when following prey or during strandings

habitat: Long-finned pilot whales prefer the deep, cold waters of the North Atlantic, typically staying in areas where the ocean floor drops to 600 feet or more. In New England waters, you're most likely to spot them on whale watching trips that venture far offshore, particularly along the continental shelf edge. They favor areas with steep underwater topography where squid and deep-water fish congregate.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in New England waters as they follow squid migrations northward. Best viewing from whale watching boats venturing into deep offshore waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings in New England as they follow food sources. Most active during cooler morning and evening hours when squid move closer to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still present in New England waters but may begin moving south. Often seen in larger groups as families merge before migration.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters as most populations move to warmer southern waters following their prey.

funFact: Long-finned pilot whales have one of the most complex social structures in the animal kingdom - daughters stay with their mothers for life, and grandmothers help raise calves, creating multi-generational family pods that can include four generations of relatives all swimming together!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with short-finned pilot whales, but long-finned pilot whales have much longer, more curved pectoral fins and prefer colder waters. Memory trick: 'Long fins, cold water' - if you're seeing pilot whales in chilly New England waters with dramatically long fins, they're almost certainly long-finned pilot whales.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'whales,' pilot whales are actually the largest members of the dolphin family. This naming confusion dates back to early whalers who classified them based on size rather than scientific relationships. They're more closely related to orcas than to true whales like humpbacks or blues.
compareHints: Long-finned pilot whales differ from their close relative, the short-finned pilot whale, primarily in their dramatically longer pectoral fins and preference for colder waters. Short-finned pilot whales stick to warmer tropical and subtropical waters and have much stubbier fins. In New England's cold North Atlantic waters, you're almost guaranteed to be seeing the long-finned species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Short-finned pilot whales differ from their close relative, the long-finned pilot whale, primarily in their flipper length and tooth count.
